0db8518d-c9f6-5aef-aca1-75a988170af8.name: Taifas
0db8518d-c9f6-5aef-aca1-75a988170af8.also_known_as: Dynasties of the central Maghreb, Iberian Peninsula
0db8518d-c9f6-5aef-aca1-75a988170af8.history:
The AH 5th / AD 11th century was a time of change in the western Mediterranean. First, the ancient world lost importance in favour of Islam, which came to dominate the shores of the Mediterranean, and second, 'territorial' towns supplanted 'imperial' towns, which were no longer needed. These 'new' towns would be dominated by small dynasties ruling over political and economic areas of differing sizes.  
The family groups that controlled these towns were generally native to the region, and their members already full converts to Islam. These dynasties usually adopted names linked to their founders. The Maghreb was dominated by dynasties such as the Zirids (who founded several towns in central Maghreb) and the Hammadids (the Banu Hammad entered into conflict with the Zirids and chased them to Ifriqiya \[Tunisia\] before taking control of central Maghreb from 408 to 547 / 1018 to 1152).  
In the Iberian Peninsula, the 5th / 11th century saw the emergence of a group of 'taifa' (flag) kingdoms, still based around family groups, that multiplied after the fall of the caliphate. These kingdoms included the Abbadids of Seville, the Aftasids of Badajoz, the Hudids of Saragossa, the Zirids of Granada and the Hammadids of Malaga. Incessant disputes between the small Taifa kings helped the progress of the Christian Reconquista from the north and the conquest of al-Andalus by the Almoravids.

0dc8430e-9925-5792-b703-2201e9d5674a.name: Alawids
0dc8430e-9925-5792-b703-2201e9d5674a.area: Morocco. Capitals: Fez, Meknes and Rabat
0dc8430e-9925-5792-b703-2201e9d5674a.history:
The greatness of the Sa'dids was disproportionately linked to exceptionally favourable circumstances and the personalities of two sovereigns: 'Abd al-Malik and Ahmad al-Mansur.  
On the death of the latter (AH 1011 / AD 1603), the political and economic difficulties resurfaced, as did the unrest of the brotherhoods and the piracy that reinforced the breakdown of relations with Europe.  
The Alawid Sharifs, who held some power in Tafilalet, used their religious power and their skill as warriors and organisers to take control of eastern Morocco before taking Fez (1076 / 1666) and then Marrakesh (1079 / 1669).  
Mulay Isma'il, the most renowned of the sultans (1082–1139 / 1672–1727), consolidated the work of the founders of the dynasty and breathed new life into Moroccan civilisation. He fought the Turks and took the places still held by the Europeans on the Atlantic. However, this military power proved to be too costly and, after the death of Mulay Isma'il, Morocco fell into a deep political and economic crisis, which worsened the effect of the loss of revenues generated through privateering.  
After 30 years of chaos, Morocco experienced a spectacular recovery under Sidi Muhammad bin 'Abdallah (1170–1204 1757–90), who regained control of the army and the tribal administration and opened the country to the Atlantic by developing Tangiers and Casablanca and founding Essaouira, as well as re-establishing diplomatic and commercial links with Europe and even setting up relations with the USA. This recovery was cut short by a plague epidemic and a great famine, with the population plunging from five to three million between 1189 and 1214 / 1776 and 1800. The country became inward-looking and its weakness left it wide open to the vast European colonial movement.

1b44d492-30f4-535f-900d-c5ef2637794f.name: Seljuqs (Anatolian)
1b44d492-30f4-535f-900d-c5ef2637794f.also_known_as: The Seljuqs of Rum or Rum-Seljuqs
1b44d492-30f4-535f-900d-c5ef2637794f.area: Anatolia (also known as Asia Minor, the Asian part of modern Turkey)
1b44d492-30f4-535f-900d-c5ef2637794f.history:
From the early AH 5th / AD 11th century, the Oghuz \[Oğuz\] Turks began making incursions into Anatolia and, following the battle of Manzikert (Malazgirt, in eastern Turkey) between the Great Seljuqs and the Byzantines in 463 / 1071, the Great Seljuq Sultan Alparslan \[Alp Arslan\] sent several Turcoman leaders and chiefs to take Anatolia. The first Turkish emirates were soon established in Anatolia: the Saltuqids in Erzurum, the Mengüjekids in Erzincan and the Danishmendids in Sivas.  
Süleyman Shah, who took Konya and the surrounding area, founded the Anatolian Seljuq state in 469 / 1077. Konya was briefly the capital, before being replaced by Iznik after it was taken by the Seljuqs in 472 / 1080. With the advent of the First Crusade in 489 / 1096, Iznik and the region returned to Byzantine rule and the Seljuqs re-established their capital at Konya.  
Having reigned solely over Konya and the surrounding area, the Seljuqs of Anatolia quickly expanded their territory. In the 7th/13th century, by installing lesser rulers in newly conquered regions, they came to control much of Anatolia, with the exception of the coastal regions of the west.  
The Anatolian Seljuq state had its political, economic and cultural heyday during the reign of Alaeddin Keykubad I \['Ala' al-Din Kay Qubadh\], 616–34/ 1220–37. The conquest of Alanya on the Mediterranean coast elevated the Seljuqs to the status of great power on the maritime trading routes, while the caravan routes that criss-crossed Anatolia enabled them to increase their power by taxing the movement of goods.  
The unification of Turkey was consolidated and public safety was assured in Anatolia. Starting with Konya, Kayseri and Sivas, the citadels of many Anatolian towns were fortified, and the towns themselves modernised and endowed with monuments. The Anatolian Seljuq state began to decline after the Babai rebellions during the reign of Gıyaseddin Keyhüsrev II \[Giyath al-Din Kay Khusraw, 634–44 / 1237–46) in 640 / 1242 and defeat to the Mongols at the Battle of Kösedag \[Köse Dagh\] in 641 / 1243. After that, Anatolia was governed by the Mongols. The death of Sultan Gıyaseddin Mesud III \[Giyath al-Din Masud\] in 708 / 1308 marked the official end of the Seljuq State.

2cf9d6c6-0226-5c5d-8710-c052cc2ac4c7.name: Al-Busaid
2cf9d6c6-0226-5c5d-8710-c052cc2ac4c7.history:
The Al Busaid dynasty, also known as the House of Al Said, was a line of rulers that included the Sultanate of Oman (1744-1856), the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman (1856-1970) and the Sultanate of Zanzibar (1856-1964). Founded by Ahmad bin Said al- Busaidi, ruler of Oman and the east African territories, the Al Busaid dynasty governed the region for 250 years. During Ahmad bin Said al- Busaidi’s 39-year reign, the Omani navy was a formidable presence in the Indian Ocean, second only to the British navy. It very easily expelled the Persian forces from the region while protecting Ottoman ships in the Gulf of Oman and the Indian Ocean.  
  
The modern history of Oman has witnessed two different systems of governance: the *imama* system and the sultanate system. An *imamah* (imamate) can refer to the office of the imam or to his spiritual leadership. Imams are spiritual leaders who may exercise control over a particular region. To receive the *imamah*, a ruler has to be elected.  
  
Imam Ahmed ibn Said (1741-1783) established the sultanate system during his rule. It was the first time that a separation was established between the two political systems. He saved Oman from a civil war, restored it to its regional place in the Afro-Asian and maritime system and made a decisive contribution to the shaping of Oman’s modern history - a history of the sultanate as opposed to the *imama* system. In 1741, he received the *imamah*. Ahmed was remarkable for his firm attitude towards colonial hegemony. This became apparent when he barred the East India Company from setting up a branch in Muscat. The long reign of Ahmed ibn Said (about 39 years) also witnessed changes and new tendencies in Omani society. His reign not only forged a new vision of a political system but also helped lay the foundation of a new political, national and cultural identity.  
  
Ahmed ibn Said died in 1778 and was succeeded by his son, Said bin Ahmed, a pious leader who divided duties among palace officials along religious, administrative and military lines. Said bin Ahmed kept his *imamah* and moved to al-Rustaq, where he remained until his death in 1811. In 1783, his son, Hamad bin Said, decided to move his court to the coastal city of Muscat and make the city his political capital. He also took the title of sultan, signalling his power.  
  
Hamad bin Said was a capable ruler who did much for the country in his eight-year reign. He facilitated reform policy in the initial stages of the transition but died suddenly in 1792. On his death, Oman’s political system was divided into three main parts: Said bin Ahmed, the official imam, stayed in al-Rustaq; Sayyid Sultan bin Ahmed (who succeeded Hamad ibn Said) retained Muscat as his base of power; and finally, Sayf, Ahmed ibn Sa’id’s third son, took the city of Sohar (located near Hormuz) as his centre of power. Thus in 1793, and with the collaboration of the British, the Islamic state of Oman, which had been a unified nation, was now fragmented into three separate polities.  
  
After his accession to the throne in 1792, Sayyid Sultan ibn Ahmed (1792-1804) used his power and intellect to restore Muscat to the place it was under the rule of his father Ahmed. Oman became an ally of France in the region east of Africa and the Indian Ocean, especially as Britain was beginning to appear a hazard to Oman, India and all the countries of the Gulf.  
  
Sayyid Said bin Sultan, aged 17, came to power in 1806 on his father’s death and remained ruler for half a century until his death in 1856. He was the first sayyid of Oman, received the title of sultan and was also called ‘the Great’. Oman was established as a major commercial and maritime power in the Indian Ocean during his reign. He was succeeded by Thuwaini bin Said al-Said, who was the third son of Said bin Sultan and ruled from 1856-1866.  
  
Between 1866 and 1970, Oman experienced the reign of six other rulers. Finally, from 1970 to 2020, Oman was ruled by Sultan Qaboos, who modernized the region. The current heir to the throne since 2020 is Sultan Haitham bin Tariq.  
  
Bibliography  
• Ghubash, Hussein, Oman - The Islamic Democratic Tradition, London and New York: Routledge, 2006.  
• Jones, Jeremy and Ridout, Nicholas, A History of Modern Oman, Cambridge (UK) and New York: Cambridge University Press, 2016.  
  
This profile, compiled by Fiza Ishaq and copy-edited by Adrienne Staudohar, was added as part of the ‘Explore Islamic Art Collections’ project.

31ce1f02-7f90-58b4-be58-74a7ce5f450b.name: House of Muhammad Ali
31ce1f02-7f90-58b4-be58-74a7ce5f450b.history:
Egypt remained one of the provinces under the Ottoman Empire for three centuries (AH 923–1220 / AD 1517–1805). However, the French Expedition to Egypt led by Napoleon Bonaparte in 1213 / 1798 marked the end of direct Ottoman rule in Egypt.  
In 1218 / 1803 Muhammad Ali, the military leader of the Albanian Ottoman army, by order of the Ottoman sultan, succeeded in evacuating the French army from Egypt, and was appointed as ruler of the country by a decree from the Ottoman Sultan. The right of succession was granted to his progeny by another decree in 1257 / 1841. Thus Egypt became an independent state under the *wali* (governor) Muhammad Ali.  
A great reform and development movement was initiated by the new ruler. Canals were dug, bridges restored, schools established, and factories of all kinds spread all over the country. A large number of mosques, *sabils* (drinking fountains) and palaces were constructed by foreign architects and workers, which allowed new elements to appear in architecture and decoration. Buildings were erected from wood and brick instead of stone, and the traditional fine marble mosaics were replaced by white marble and alabaster; *mashrabiyyas* (screens) were replaced by modern windows. Decorations based on flowers, grape clusters and landscape paintings in the Rococo style appeared. Such artistic elements, brought over from Europe by Italian artists, were common in Turkey in the 12th / 18th centuries. The Turkish artists, however, adapted this new style to suit local taste and the best Islamic traditions.  
The line of rulers succeeding Muhammad 'Ali included 'Abbas I (1264–70 / 1848–54), Sa'id (1270–80 / 1854–63), who initiated the digging of the Suez Canal, and Isma'il (r. 1280–96 / 1863–79 d. 1312 / 1895), who undertook the architectural development of Cairo, on the occasion of the Suez Canal inauguration, to make it an image of Paris, with gardens such as al-Azbakiyya and an opera house. He built Abdeen Palace to which he moved the seat of rule from the Citadel.  
The last of this dynasty's kings was Faruq I (1355–71 / 1936–52), a great-grandson of Muhammad 'Ali, whose deposition from the throne in 1371 / 1952 in the 23 July Revolution brought to an end the reign of this house.

356a10dc-13a5-5628-a58c-94f3d80361e7.name: Kingdom of Mysore
356a10dc-13a5-5628-a58c-94f3d80361e7.history:
The kingdom of Mysore was established after the defeat of the Vijayanagara emperor and the end of the empire (founded in 1336) in a battle with the Deccan Sultanates in 1565. The emperor of the Vijayanagara empire was killed and the capital city was completely sacked. There began an era of political instability in southern India when the Wodeyars and other minor chiefs and kings sought independence and vied for power in the region. There was incessant fighting with rulers of neighbouring territories, often futile. The early 20th century was a period of incessant warfare in the region as the Marathas, the Mughals and the Nizam all sent their armies and fought to plunder as much as possible.  
  
At its earliest, Mysore was a petty chiefdom ruled by Bettada Chamaraja Wodeyar from 1513 to 1553. The territory comprised of the town of Mysore and a few adjoining villages. It was located in the Southern Maidan region of the modern state of Karnataka. From 1578 to 1617, Mysore was ruled by Raja Wodeyar, who established the kingdom by becoming Vijayanagara’s viceroy at Srirangapatna in 1610. They worked hard to establish Mysore as Vijayanagara’s successor state.  
  
In the 17th century, Mysore was independent of Vijayanagara, and Chikkadevaraja Wodeyar was the regnant ruler (between 1673 and 1704). He expanded the kingdom, despite attacks from the Mughals, Maratha, Ikkeri and Madura. Chikkadevaraja entered in a partnership with the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, which led to a period of peace in the region. By the late 17th century, the territory of Mysore was a war-torn landscape divided into many administrative regions by the Vijayanagara rulers, and it eventually came to be ruled by local men descended from and representing influential lineages.  
  
During the 18th century, the rulers of Mysore were subjugated under the dalavoys or prime ministers of the kingdom. They looked out for their own interests rather than to the betterment of the kingdom. In the late 1750s, the Dalavoy Nanjirajaraiya was forced to retire. His authority was not passed on to the king of Mysore; rather it was passed on to Haidar Ali, who was an officer in the Mysore army. He became the Mysore dalavoy in 1761 and took the power and authority of the king whose role was mostly ritualistic and ceremonial. Haidar Ali did much for the kingdom and its army, which he reorganised and brought to a level with the Europeans, and he worked towards the expansion of the kingdom. As the dalavoy, Haidar Ali and later, his son and successor Tipu Sultan fought four wars with the British.  
  
Tipu Sultan came to power in 1782, after the death of his father Haider Ali. There were constant clashes between the rulers of Mysore and the British at Madras, who were active in Indian politics in the second half of the 18th century. As a result of the Treaty of Paris in 1763, the British were more powerful in India over the French. In the later 17th century, Mysore also fought in wars against other Indian rulers. However, the Anglo-Mysore wars were momentous, as the last war fought in 1799 led to the siege of Srirangapatna and the death of the powerful ruler Tipu Sultan. It also resulted in the establishment of Mysore as a “princely state,” a nominal sovereign in British India. The heroic status of Tipu Sultan was a consequence of his stand against the British presence in the region and to protect his capital Seringapatam. Towards the end of the 18th century, the Mysore kingdom under Tipu Sultan included parts of the modern states of Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.  
  
After the death of Tipu Sultan, the British re-established the Wodeyars to the throne of Mysore and installed a British resident in the royal court. The Wodeyar ruled Mysore until 1947 when it was accessioned to the new independent republic of India. Mysore, which continued to be ruled by its former ruler until 1974, became a part of Karnataka state post-independence.  
  
This profile, compiled by Fiza Ishaq and copy-edited by Emily Richey was added as part of the ‘Explore Islamic Art Collections’ project.

5be23b1b-ff3d-5174-b866-6358dc1299f4.name: Sassanids
5be23b1b-ff3d-5174-b866-6358dc1299f4.area: Persia, Iraq, Afghanistan, Anatolia, Jordan, Bahrain, Egypt and Syria (under Roman rule)
5be23b1b-ff3d-5174-b866-6358dc1299f4.history:
The Sasanian empire was the second Persian empire to rule Iran (224-651) and one of the largest and most powerful empires of late antiquity. The dynasty was known as Eranshahr (or Iranshaehr, “dominion of the Iranians”). It was the last great Iranian empire before the conquest of Iran by the Muslims and a period of great importance and significance in Iran. Sasanian Iran was considered to have influenced empires and civilizations, such as the Romans, well beyond its borders and as far as Western Europe, Africa, China and India.  
  
The dynasty was founded by Ardashir I, whose father, Pabag, ruled a small town named Khair. During his reign, Pabag attempted several campaigns to conquer Iran, particularly in the period from 205 to 206. Pabag rebelled against the local kings in the homeland of the Sasanians. He had planned for his son, Shapur, to become the first Sasanian ruler; however, when Shapur died in unknown circumstances, Ardashir was left to conquer Fars and beyond.  
  
Ardashir appointed his son, also named Shapur, as co-regent following a conflict with the Roman empire and then retired to his home province. According to some ancient Manichaean religious writing, the prophet Mani made his first appearance during the rule of Shapur. Impressed with the ruler, he composed a text known as “Shabuhragan”, in Shapur’s name.  
Shapur was succeeded first by Hormizd I (270–71) and later Wahram I (271–74), but both of them ruled for a short time and little is known about them. Wahram II took the throne after a conspiracy in the imperial administration. He was called “king of Sakas”, a title which conveyed the might of the Sasanians compared to the Iranian-speaking people of the east.  
Narseh, the son of Shapur, functioned as the king of Armenia. The rule of Narseh (293–302) coincided with the coming of Christianity to Armenia. After Narseh’s death in 302, his son, Hormizd II, took the throne. Hormizd was in turn succeeded by his son, Adur-Narseh, who ruled for a short time in 309.  
  
Shapur II was the longest reigning monarch of the Sasanian dynasty. He is considered a legendary monarch who was crowned while in his mother’s womb, exactly 40 days after the death of his father, Hormizd II. Another son of Hormizd II, named Ardashir II, succeeded his brother Shapur II.  
  
While Shapur II was considered a legendary monarch, his successor, Shapur III, was a weaker ruler, and the period of his reign is considered a temporary waning of Sasanian royal power. Another son of Shapur II, Wahram IV, ruled for a short time (388–99). Wahram IV was removed by court nobles who favoured his son, Yazdgerd I, who became known as the one who restored the Sasanian empire.  
  
Yazdgerd I was succeeded by his son, Wahram V (420–38). Wahram V’s reign has been romanticised in classical Persian literature in a collection of interconnected stories called “Haft Peykar” by the poet Nezami (12th century). The poet’s imaginary stories may have been drawn from actual Sasanian period romances.  
  
Yazdgerd II (438–57) then succeeded his father. He was unlike his grandfather in that he was not tolerant of Christianity, particularly in Armenia. His two sons, Hormizd III (457–59) and Peroz (459–84), ruled consecutively. Peroz is said to have ousted his brother to gain the throne.  
  
Peroz’s rule was briefly followed by his brother Walakhsh (484–88) who ruled for a short duration and was replaced by Peroz’s son, Kawad I (488–97, 499–531). During Kawad’s rule, the Sasanian dynasty was faced with economic and political instability. Kawad briefly lost his throne to Zamasp (497–99) but later regained it with the assistance of the Hephthalites.  
  
Khosrow I Anusheruwan’s reign (531–79) has been noted as a high point in the history of the Sasanian dynasty. *Xwarrah* or “glory” is the essence of Iranian royal ideology and has been demonstrated in the *Avesta* (sacred book); it is the precondition of rightful rule. It recognizes Ahura Mazda, the one supreme being, the deity of wisdom. This glory may be granted or withheld from Iranian rulers and evil characters in accordance with the judgment of Ahura Mazda and other gods such as Ohrmazd and deities such as the goddess of fertility, Lady Anahita. These gods are said to bestow glory on the *shahanshah* (“king of kings”). Such ideals and ideologies are believed to have been formed during the reign of Khosrow I as a consequence of the interest taken by the Sasanian court and society in writing. During this time, historical tales and the history of kings were compiled in the *Khuday-namag* (the “Book of the Lords”).  
Hormizd IV (579–90) did not last long on the throne. He was deposed in favour of his son, Khosrow II Aparvez (590-628) who in turn was succeeded by Wahram Chobin, a warrior known for his heroic accomplishment in a war with the Hephthalites. He declared himself emperor and took the name Wahram VI. This was the first time that someone who did not belong to the Sasanian dynasty had declared rule over Sasanian territory. In the mid-620s, the situation was reversed after an attack by Heraclius of the Roman empire. In 628, Kavad II acceded to the throne, but his short reign was riddled with chaos as well as a plague, known as the plague of Shiroye.  
  
During the final phase of Sasanian rule, there was disunion and factionalism at court. Ardashir III (628-29), the son of Kavad II, was a child. He was soon removed from the throne by one of the Byzantine commanders, Shahrbaraz. However, courtiers were not in his favour; they removed him and made Boran (628–630/1), a daughter of Khosrow II, the ruler. She was soon replaced by another daughter of Khosrow II, Azarmigduxt (around 630–31). Finally, in 632, Yazdgerd III (632–51), grandson of Khosrow II, was installed on the throne. It was during Yazdgerd III’s rule that the Sasanian empire was conquered by the Muslims, in 637.  
  
Bibliography  
• Daryaee, Touraj, Sasanian Persia. The Rise and Fall of an Empire, London: I. B. Tauris, 2009.  
  
This profile, compiled by Fiza Ishaq and copy-edited by Adrienne Staudohar, was added as part of the ‘Explore Islamic Art Collections’ project.

9edc1c13-a45a-5e4f-b590-717688101260.name: Abbasids
9edc1c13-a45a-5e4f-b590-717688101260.area: Ifriqiya [Tunisia], Jordan, Egypt, North Africa, Iraq
9edc1c13-a45a-5e4f-b590-717688101260.history:
The Abbasid era is considered to be the golden age of Islamic civilisation. The Abbasids were able to establish their supremacy by taking up the cause of non-Arabs who had been unjustly treated by the Umayyads and who, under the leadership of the rebel Abu Muslim al-Khurasani, successfully overthrew them in AH 132 / AD 750. The Abbasids became the caliphs of the Islamic empire that same year.  
The outer reaches of the empire were stabilised and consolidated by Caliph al-Mansur (AH 136–7 / AD 754–75) who broke up the monopoly of the Arabs over the political and economic institutions of the state and encouraged equality between the different groups that made up Abbasid society. Construction of the new capital, Baghdad, was completed in AH 138 / AD 766.  
The Abbasid period reached its zenith during the reign of Caliph Harun al-Rashid (AH 169–93 / AD 786–809) who achieved peace with Byzantium and exchanged embassies with Charlemagne of France. This period included the reigns of al-Ma'mun (AH 197–218 / AD 813–33), al-Mu'tasim (AH 218–27 / AD 833–42) and al-Wathiq (AH 227–32 / AD 842–7).  
The new wealth created by the switch from an agrarian to a trading economy reduced the social disparity between Arab and non-Arab communities and promoted the development of numerous craft industries, such as glass, ceramics and textiles, exported via the old trade routes from China to sub-Saharan Africa. Learning was encouraged and the key texts of Greek, Persian and Indian civilisations were translated into Arabic. Numerous great scholars furthered all fields of knowledge: philosophy (al-Kindi and al-Farabi), astronomy, mathematics (al-Khawarizmi), medicine (al-Razi and Ibn Sina), physics and chemistry (Ibn Sina), and their contributions would go on to influence the whole of medieval thinking.  
Abbasid power began to decline in the AH 5th / AD 11th century, and several provinces became independent. The Fatimids (AH 296–566 / AD 909–1171) established a rival caliphate in Egypt and Syria, and Tughrul (Tughril) Beg emerged from the Turkish regiments of the Abbasid army to take Baghdad in AH 447 / AD 1055. The final blow was dealt to the Abbasid Dynasty by the Mongols who swept through the Middle East and took Baghdad in AH 656 / AD 1258.

ab22ae48-7fde-5229-a684-189558585904.name: Nasrids
ab22ae48-7fde-5229-a684-189558585904.history:
When the Almohad Caliph al-Ma'mun, enthroned in Seville in AH 624 / AD 1227, returned to Morocco, a member of the vizier Banu al-Ahmar family, Muhammad bin Yusuf bin Nasr, proclaimed himself king (627 / 1230) founding the Nasrid dynasty, which ruled Granada until 897 / 1492.  
He stayed in power by paying an annual tribute to the king of Castile and assisted passively in the breathtaking progress of the Christian Reconquista, with the surrender of Córdoba (633 / 1236), Jaen and Arjona (643 / 1246), and Seville (645 / 1248).  
Thanks to their plotting and dealing and the occasional military support of the Marinids, the Nasrids experienced a veritable golden age, the most stunning examples of which being the Alhambra and the Generalife. This splendour lasted until 886 / 1482 when Boabdil (Abu 'Abdallah) overthrew his father but failed to contain the Reconquista. Malaga fell in 892 / 1487; Baeza and Almeria in 894 / 1489, among other places. He ended up capitulating, and the Catholic kings entered Granada on 2 January 1492, closing the book on the epic that was 'al-Andalus'.  
The existence of al-Andalus as a Muslim political entity lasted nearly 800 years, but the Reconquista, which began in 722 (Battle of Pelayo / Covadonga) lasted nearly 900, continuing to 1610 with successive waves of expulsions of 'moriscos'.  
However, although al-Andalus ceased to exist as a political entity, its cultural and artistic influence lived on in Spain, where Mudejar art conditioned architectural thought until the 18th century, and in Morocco, where Hispano-Moorish architecture and craftsmanship successfully combined Hispano-Visigothic art with traits of the Muslim West and the Berbers, the latter having survived through the Sharif dynasties.

b372ff12-6d26-5b7b-84e0-c0679b12cfbb.name: Umayyads
b372ff12-6d26-5b7b-84e0-c0679b12cfbb.area: Syria, Asia Minor, Egypt, North Africa, Iraq, Iran, Central Asia, Iberian Peninsula
b372ff12-6d26-5b7b-84e0-c0679b12cfbb.history:
Founded in AH 41 / AD 661 by Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan of the Bani Umayya family, the Umayyad dynasty was the first Islamic dynasty after the death of the Prophet Muhammad and the caliphs who succeeded him in 11 / 632. The most important Umayyad caliphs were Mu'awiya (41–60 / 661–80), 'Abd al-Malik (65–86 / 685–705) and Hisham (105–25 / 724–43). Under al-Walid I (86–96 / 705–15), military conquests reached as far as Spain and central Europe, while in the east the Umayyad kingdom extended to Transoxania and northern India. In 132 / 750, the Umayyad dynasty was overthrown by the Abbasids.  
During the Umayyad caliphate, many failed attacks were launched against Constantinople and the Byzantine Empire. In Spain, the Visigoths were defeated in 92 / 711, but the Muslim advance in central Europe was halted in 114 / 732 by Charles Martel at the Battle of Poitiers.  
The Umayyad dynasty introduced the idea of hereditary rulership in Islam and contributed many eminent figures to the caliphate from its family ranks.  
With the arrival of the Umayyads, the centre of political power in Islam shifted from Madina in the Arabian Peninsula to Syria, with Damascus becoming the new capital of the caliphate. This change had both political and cultural repercussions.  
Borrowing administrative practices from both the Byzantines and the Sassanids, the Umayyad caliphs became talented rulers, capable of controlling the first Islamic empire, which spread over a wide area thanks to its military successes.  
Social tensions quickly became apparent among non-Arab converts who, contrary to the teaching of Islam, did not enjoy the same rights as Arab Muslims. Rebellions in southern Jordan, Iraq and eastern Iran led to the gradual collapse of the dynasty.  
The Umayyads were energetic builders; their architects, artists and craftsmen were responsible for the towns, palaces, mosques and works of art that today symbolise the rich history of the early years of Islam.

b812e3d9-24d7-5ef1-bfc7-8031d0fa5144.name: Ayyubids
b812e3d9-24d7-5ef1-bfc7-8031d0fa5144.area: Egypt, Syria, southeastern Anatolia, Jazira, Yemen
b812e3d9-24d7-5ef1-bfc7-8031d0fa5144.history:
Events arising from the arrival in Baghdad of the leader of the Seljuq Turks in AH 446 / AD 1055 led to the Crusades and the invasion of Jerusalem in 492 / 1099. However, this did not prevent the Seljuqs from becoming the most powerful force in the Muslim world at that time.  
During the 5th / 11th century, faced with conflict with the Seljuq Turks and the Fatimids, the Seljuqs recruited *atabegs*, military commanders, as regional governors. In 468 / 1076, the Atabeg Atsiz, took Damascus from the Fatimids. In the 6th / 12th century, the powerful Zangid Dynasty reunified Syria. Nur al-Din, son of the founder of the Zangid dynasty, conquered Damascus in 548 / 1154, and his lieutenant Salah al-Din (Saladin) destroyed the Fatimid caliphate in 566 / 1171 and ended the Latin occupation of Jerusalem in 579 / 1187.  
The Atabegs and the Ayyubids introduced far-reaching changes to their realm, building numerous *madrasas* (schools) for the orthodox re-education of their subjects. With unprecedented levels of construction, the Seljuq period brought about a renaissance for Aleppo and Damascus, with the reconstruction of the Great Mosque and the foundation of the citadel in Damascus and the construction of mosques, *hammams* (baths), *madrasas*, *turbes* (mausoleums), *khanqahs* (hostels) and *ribats* (fortresses).  
The Zangid and Ayyubid princes managed to drive the crusaders from Edessa (Urfa) in 540 / 1146 and consolidated their hold on the region with the conquest of Egypt in 566 / 1171.  
In the middle of the 6th / 12th century, under Nur al-Din and his Ayyubid successors, Damascus again became a major centre of the Muslim world and prospered in all areas of society. As capital of an independent state, it came to assume all of the characteristics of a great city.  
From the 5th to the 7th centuries / 11th to the 13th centuries a number of factors favoured the development of art and urban activity. Artuqids, Zangids, Seljuqs of Rum and Ayyubids left their mark in various media, from pottery and metalwork to book arts and architecture. From the sober, classical forms of Ayyubid architecture to the brilliant decorative arts, this key period is characterised by high-quality artistic output, having the same importance for Syria as the Mamluk period for Egypt, or the Ottoman period for Turkey.

b866c59b-f81b-5655-972c-c4ac569b959e.name: Mughal
b866c59b-f81b-5655-972c-c4ac569b959e.history:
In Perso-Arab language the term Mughal means “the Mongol” or the “Mongolians”. Babur, the founder of the Mughal Dynasty who ruled from 1526 to 1530, was of Timurid–Mongolian heritage. On his paternal side he was a descendant of the warlord Amir Timur or Tamerlane, a fierce warrior of the late 14th and early 15th centuries, and on the maternal side of the family he was a descendant of Genghis Khan. Babur conquered a large territory extending from central Asia to the shores of the Mediterranean.  
  
By the late 15th century, the Mughals had begun patronizing the arts, commissioning the construction of imposing architecture and making grand illuminated manuscripts. They were considered refined and sophisticated. It was in 1526 at the battle of Panipat that Babur had a huge victory; he conquered northern India up to the Gangetic Plain after a struggle with Afghans, the Lodi Sultan of Delhi and the Rajputs under Rana Sanga of Mewar. In order to legitimise his rule, Babur went on to build three mosques.  
Babur died in 1530 and was succeeded by this son, Humayun, who inherited a territory that was yet to be consolidated. After being defeated by the Afghan chief of Bihar, Shir Shah Suri, Humayun was driven to the Persian court of the Iranian-Safavid court ruler, Shah Tahmasp I. With the help of the Persian emperor, he reconquered northern India in 1555. He died in 1556, in Delhi.  
  
Humayun’s son, Akbar, acceded to the throne at the young age of 12 years, and he went on to rule for nearly 50 years (1556–1605). Akbar is considered a very important ruler of the Mughal dynasty. Most significant were his many achievements; he set up an enduring foundation for Mughal governance, created inclusive policies and adopted an attitude of tolerance towards non-Muslims. This method of governing made him an amicable ruler and created a state that was syncretic in character.  
  
By the time Akbar passed away in 16o5, he had built a consolidated empire that would flourish under the rule of his son, Jahangir, and grandson, Shah Jahan. Jahangir followed the practices that Akbar had commenced during his reign. He had acceded to the throne in 1602 after clashing with his father and masterminding the death of Akbar’s close advisor, Abu al-Fazl, who he thought was against Jahangir becoming the heir. In 1611, he married a woman named Nur Jahan. She was a powerful, intelligent person who took the reins of the empire when Jahangir was ill.  
  
During its last phase, the Mughal empire was ruled by Nur Jahan and her family. One of these rulers was Prince Khurram, later known as Shah Jahan, a well-known military strategist. He was the one responsible for Jahangir’s victory during his reign. In 1614 he led a campaign against the Sisodiya Rajput fortress of Chittor and forced Rana Amar Singh to surrender. Jahangir was pleased with this victory and considered Khurram as heir apparent.  
  
Under Shah Jahan’s rule, the Mughal empire was prosperous, wealthy and internationally renowned. In the first 12 years of his reign, Shah Jahan pursued several military campaigns in a bid to subdue recalcitrant rulers. At the same time, he conquered territory in eastern India, Sind and the northwest. In 1636, he made a breakthrough in his campaign in order to increase territorial expansion into the Deccan. The Mughals signed a treaty with two dynasties of the Deccan, namely, Adil Shah of Bijapur and the Qutb Shahs of Golkonda. This resulted in 20 years of the Mughals’ peaceful coexistence with the Deccan Sultanates.  
  
In 1658, Shah Jahan’s son, Aurangzeb, ruled the Mughal empire from 1658 to 1707. He became the victorious leader after a battle of succession in which two of his brothers were killed, one brother was exiled to Burma and his father was imprisoned. His reign lasted for 49 years. He was known as Alamgir, the seizer of the world. His top achievement was to expand Mughal territory all the way to the Deccan. He subjugated the sultans of the Deccan and brought about a massive expansion of the empire.  
  
Aurangzeb has been considered an orthodox Muslim who broke away from the liberal traditions of his predecessors. Contrary to the image that has been painted, Aurangzeb was an Indian ruler who strove throughout his life to preserve and expand the Mughal empire, gain political power, and rule with his own vision of justice.  
  
The court of the Mughal successors was known for its aristocratic high culture. These rulers enjoyed entertainment in the form of music and poetry, commissioned miniature paintings and objects, and supported the construction of monumental architecture for the imperial Mughal court.  
  
From 1707 to 1857, however, the Mughal dynasty was in a period of decline. Aurangzeb’s death brought with it much turmoil due to courtiers vying with each other to gain power. Bahadur Shah I (1643–1712) attempted to alter the court’s religious policies and reform its administration. After his death in 1712, the empire was involved in feuds over who would be the next successor. He was ultimately succeeded by the 20th ruler of the Mughal dynasty, Bahadur Shah Zafar or Bahadur Shah II (1837–57). However, the last Mughal emperor had no power over the kingdom; rather, he was an emperor in title alone. Throughout the 18th century north India was at the mercy of indigenous and foreign power. The arrival of the East India Company marked the end of Mughal rule. By this time the Mughal empire existed in name only, while the East India Company governed the empire.  
  
Bibliography  
• Asher, Catherine B. and Talbot, Cynthia, India before Europe, UK: Cambridge University Press, 2006.  
• Koch, Ebba, Mughal Architecture, UK: Oxford University Press, 1991.  
• Richards, John F., Gordon Johnson, The Mughal Empire, UK: Cambridge University Press, 1993.  
• Truschke, Audrey, Aurangzeb: the Man and the Myth, India: Penguin Random House India Pvt. Ltd, 2018.  
  
This profile, compiled by Fiza Ishaq and copy-edited by Adrienne Staudohar, was added as part of the ‘Explore Islamic Art Collections’ project.

c86e40a5-f47d-5f06-8a89-26f52f632eb0.name: Fatimids
c86e40a5-f47d-5f06-8a89-26f52f632eb0.history:
The assassination of Caliph 'Ali in the Iraqi city of Kufa, and of Imam Husayn, grandson of the Prophet, at Karbala, gave rise to Shi'ism, which is based on a belief in the right of the descendants of Muhammad to assume the caliphate. Opposed by the Umayyads and then the Abbasids, the movement nonetheless spread quickly through the Muslim world to reach the Maghreb, from where the Shi'a Muslims decided to conquer the great caliphate of the Muslim world. Brought to power by the missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i, Imam al-Mahdi ousted the Aghlabid Dynasty in AH 297 / AD 910 before taking Tunisia, Libya, eastern Algeria and Sicily.  
In 358 / 969, strengthened by the country's economic prosperity and stability, the Fatimid Caliph al-Mu'izz (r. 341–64 / 953–75) attempted to reconquer the East and was victorious in Egypt, leaving Ifriqiya \[Tunisia\] to the Zirids, who quickly abandoned Shi'ism for Sunnism, an act violently repressed by the Hilalian tribes that attacked the country.  
The new Fatimid capital, Cairo, became the cradle of a brilliant civilisation, bolstered by territorial conquests in Syria and Palestine. Until Salah al-Din (Saladin) finally seized power from them in 566 / 1171, the Fatimid caliphs promoted urban development, the sciences, art and literature.  
The Fatimids founded several towns including Mahdiyya and Sabra al-Mansuriyya in Ifriqiya, Achir in central Maghreb and Cairo in Egypt. In accordance with their philosophy and faith, towns were no longer organised around the mosque, but around the palace of the caliph as a symbol of power. Porticoes also began to appear in the courtyards of mosques with offset corridors in prayer rooms for the glorified procession of the caliph.  
The sciences, art, mathematics, medicine and exegesis developed spectacularly under the Fatimids, as did applied arts and crafts. Glass and ivory figures of humans and animals remain the most well known.

d9aed700-4f88-5eae-b943-d855a671e948.name: Qajar
d9aed700-4f88-5eae-b943-d855a671e948.area: Persia (Iran), Georgia and Armenia (subsequently lost to the Russian Protectorate and ultimately the British Empire)
d9aed700-4f88-5eae-b943-d855a671e948.history:
The Qajars were of Turkoman origin, based near Astarabad in northeastern Iran. The Qajar dynasty ruled Iran from 1785 to 1925. During this time, the Qajars unified Iran, promoting and encouraging new innovations in technology (such as the telegraph and railroads). The arts also flourished under their reign; photography and lithography, along with innovative forms of portraiture and oil painting brought from the West, were enthusiastically adopted by artists and patrons alike. In the 140 years that the Qajar dynasty ruled, Iran was transformed from feuding tribal confederations to a centralized monarchy and finally to a constitutional parliament. In the historical consciousness of the people, the Qajars invoked the glorious Safavid era with all its might and splendour.  
  
The first Qajar shah was Agha Mohammad Shah (1795–98). His main concern at the time of his rule was to consolidate the country’s position against its opponents, the Zands of Shiraz (1750–94). He defeated the last Zand prince, Lotf Ali Khan. Finally, Agha Mohammad Khan was assassinated by one of his attendants in May 1796 and was succeeded by his nephew, Baba Khan, who was crowned and given the name Fath ‘Ali Shah.  
Fath ‘Ali Shah ruled from 1797 to 1834. He worked on redefining the Qajar imperial image and distinguishing it from that of his predecessors. In the 37 years that Fath ‘Ali Shah reigned, he united his fellow citizens and worked to better the growing administration of the country. This was the time of the first Russo-Persian war, when Iran’s territories of Georgia and Azerbaijan were taken by rivals. The political situation with Russia and Britain was not always agreeable. A second Russo-Persian war began in the summer of 1826 in the Caucasus where Muslims fought against the Russians. After this war Iran was able to recover all its lost territories.  
  
Fath ‘Ali Shah died in 1834 and was succeeded by his grandson, Mohammad Shah (1834–48). However, Mohammad Shah’s accession led to a feud with two of his uncles, Zel al-Soltan, governor of Tehran, and Farman Farma in Fars. Each of them believed that they deserved to be successors of Fath ‘Ali Shah. Russia and Britain recognized Mohammad Shah as the successor, and he was helped and advised by Abol Qasem Qa’em Maqam, his father’s minister. He was ultimately was crowned sovereign in a ceremony held in Tehran. Mohammed Shah died in September 1848. His reign had been far from peaceful as most of it was spent struggling with Britain. He was succeeded by his son, Naser al-Din Mirza.  
  
At the age of 17 years, Naser al-Din Shah (1848–96) acceded to the throne. He initiated change and modernized the capital city of Tehran. His guide was Mir Taqi Khan Amir Nezam (later known as Amir Kabir) who served as Sadr Azam. Amir Kabir implemented reforms to modernise, develop and reform the state. He also undertook to reform the financial and military systems. His most notable achievement, however, was the establishment of Dar al-Funun (Abode of Sciences), one of the first schools in Iran to be based on a Western model of teaching. He considered it a good training ground for future civil servants and military men.  
  
After the death of Naser al-Din Shah, Mozaffar al-Din Shah (1896–1906) became the new sovereign at 43 years of age. He was known as a weak ruler and was considered more lenient with his subjects compared to his father. One of his achievements was issuing the firman, a royal edict stating that he granted a Majles (consultative assembly) and that elections would be held. The elections in Tehran were speedily performed and the first Majles was opened by Mozaffar al-Din Shah on 7 October 1906. The first act of the Majles was to prepare a constitution - a first in Iranian history. This was accomplished and signed by the ruler Mozaffar al-Din Shah five days before his death in February 1907. He was succeeded by his son, Mohammad Ali Shah.  
  
Mohammad Ali Shah (1907–09) was 35 years old at the time of his accession. He was raised by a Russian tutor, which made him unpopular with Iranian nationalists who later turned against him. The Shah attempted a coup d’état in December 1907, which failed. He was criticized by officials and the general public at the Majles. In July 1907, he abdicated the throne and left it to his 12-year-old son, Ahmad Mirza.  
  
When Ahmad Shah (1909–25) became the Qajar sovereign, the northern region of the country was under occupation; the Russo-British agreement of 1907 meant that the ministers of both countries interfered in the internal affairs of Iran, particularly in designating the membership of the cabinets. During the First World War (1914–18) Iran was besieged by Russian, British and Ottoman troops. Ahmed Shah could not recover from this setback. With a coup d'état in February 1921, Reza Khan (later known as Reza Shah Pahlavi) was elected to take the place of Ahmed Shah, who was deposed by the Majles.  
  
Bibliography  
• Algar, Hamid, Religion and State in Iran 1785-1906 - The Role of the Ulama in the Qajar Period, Berkeley, CA: University of California Press, 1980.  
• Daryaee T. (ed), The Oxford Handbook of Iranian History, UK: Oxford University Press, 2012.  
• Gleave, Robert, Religion and Society in Qajar Iran, UK: Routledge Curzon Press, BIPS Persian studies series, 2005.  
  
This profile, compiled by Fiza Ishaq and copy-edited by Adrienne Staudohar, was added as part of the ‘Explore Islamic Art Collections’ project.

f1cbe826-876f-50ce-b965-80fab0039660.name: Ottomans
f1cbe826-876f-50ce-b965-80fab0039660.area: Anatolia, Balkans, Arab lands from Iraq to Algeria
f1cbe826-876f-50ce-b965-80fab0039660.history:
The Ottoman Dynasty, which ruled for more than 600 years over the eastern Mediterranean, represents an important period of world history in the region and beyond. The Ottoman Emirate, one of the emirates of western Anatolia, burst onto the stage of history in AH 698 / AD 1299 with Osman \['Uthman\] Bey, who quickly extended his territories by signing treaties with other emirates, or by declaring war on them, during a chaotic period for Anatolia in the AH 8th and 9th / AD 14th and 15th centuries.  
The Ottomans also survived the Mongols and established themselves as a considerable force in the region. With their army and the invincible armada of the navy, the Ottomans took Istanbul in AH 856 / AD 1453 and created an empire. Their supremacy reached its peak during the reign of Süleyman the Legislator (also known as the Magnificent), AH 926–73 / AD 1520–66, when their empire stretched to Europe, the Middle East and North Africa.  
With its abundance of different influences, the Ottomans built a cultural empire that strove to establish, defend and promote interaction between the elements that made up its ethnic and religious mosaic. Its eastern character dominated until the AH 12th / AD 18th century, when political changes made it susceptible to winds of change from the West, which really took hold in the AH 13th / AD 19th century.  
During its ascendancy the empire managed to forge effective relationships with other states, but during its decline, pressures from outside seriously weakened the empire and led to its eventual destruction. Furthermore, the reforms of the AH 13th / AD 19th century never really took hold, and enlightened reformists were often beaten down by religious dogmatism. During this process the subjection of the people to the absolute power of the sultan, which retarded the emergence of critical voices, and the limited development of education, contributed to this 'global empire' taking its place in the pages of history.
